chapter_note.about: Principal component analysis finds the directions along which a cloud of data is most spread out, then describes each point using only the first few of them. It never looks at labels. This chapter covers what PCA is and is not, centring and the covariance matrix, the PCs as eigenvectors, the explained variance ratio, projection and reconstruction, the link to the SVD, and three edge cases: spherical data, scale, and the rank limit.

concept_map.title: What PCA is (and is not)
concept_map.one_line: Unsupervised, linear dimensionality reduction. It keeps the direction of most spread and ignores labels.

concept_map.title: Centring and the covariance matrix
concept_map.one_line: Subtract the means, then Sigma = X_c^T X_c / (n-1). The divisor scales eigenvalues, not directions.

concept_map.title: Principal components as eigenvectors
concept_map.one_line: PC k is the k-th eigenvector. The variance along it is lambda_k. All PCs are at 90 degrees.

concept_map.title: Explained variance ratio
concept_map.one_line: lambda_k over the trace. Add from the top to find how many PCs reach a target.

concept_map.title: Projection and reconstruction
concept_map.one_line: Score z = u.(x - mu), rebuild mu + z u. The mean squared error is the dropped eigenvalues.

concept_map.title: PCA and SVD
concept_map.one_line: X_c = U S V^T. PCs are V, lambda = sigma^2 / (n-1), scores are U S.

concept_map.title: Spherical data and tied eigenvalues
concept_map.one_line: If Sigma = cI, any perpendicular pair is a valid set of PCs. Tied eigenvalues leave the PCs in their plane free.

concept_map.title: Scale matters: standardise first
concept_map.one_line: Rescaling a feature by c multiplies its variance by c squared. PCA is not scale-invariant.

concept_map.title: Rank limit of the covariance matrix
concept_map.one_line: Centring costs one dimension, so at most min(n-1, d) eigenvalues are non-zero.

chapter_note.simple: PCA looks at a cloud of dots and finds the best direction to view them from, the one where they look most spread out. It then finds the next best direction at a right angle, and so on. To do this it centres the data, builds a table of spreads (the covariance matrix), and picks the table's special directions (eigenvectors). Each direction's eigenvalue says how much spread it holds, and dividing by the total gives its share. You can describe each point with just its first few scores and rebuild it almost exactly. It ignores labels, it depends on the units you use, and it can have at most one fewer useful direction than the number of points.

cards.title: What PCA is (and is not)
cards.simple: Picture four friends, each described by two marks, maths and physics, plotted as dots on paper. Now you may keep only one number per friend, so you lay a stick across the dots and note where each dot's shadow falls on it. Lay the stick along the long side of the cloud and the shadows stay spread out, so the friends still look different. Lay it across the short side and the shadows pile up, so the friends look alike. PCA finds the best stick for you, and it never asks which friend belongs to which team. In exam words: PCA is unsupervised, linear dimensionality reduction. It keeps the direction of largest variance and ignores labels.
cards.idea: Say each student has two marks and you want just **one** number per student. **PCA** (principal component analysis) draws the best line through the cloud of points and replaces each point by its shadow on that line. The best line keeps the shadows as spread out as possible. It never looks at labels.
cards.definition:
PCA is an **unsupervised, linear** method for **dimensionality reduction**. It finds perpendicular unit vectors $u_1,u_2,\dots$ called principal components (PCs). The first one gives the shadows the largest variance:

$$u_1=\arg\max_{\|u\|=1}\ \operatorname{Var}\big(u^\top x\big)$$

Symbols: $x$ is a centred data point, $u^\top x$ is the length of its shadow along $u$, and $\|u\|=1$ means $u$ is a unit vector. 'arg max' means 'the $u$ that makes it largest'. 'Unsupervised' means the labels $y$ are never used. 'Linear' means each new feature is a weighted sum of the old ones. Keeping the first $k$ PCs gives the $k$-dimensional view with the smallest mean squared reconstruction error.
cards.intuition_full: Hold a pencil in front of a lamp. Sideways, its shadow shows the full length. Pointing at the wall, the shadow is a dot, and you cannot tell the pencil from a pebble. PCA picks the view that keeps the most. Spread is what lets you tell points apart, so spread is what we keep. There is a second way to see it. For each point, Pythagoras gives (shadow)$^2$ + (leftover)$^2$ = (distance from the centre)$^2$. Added over all points, kept spread + lost spread = a fixed total, so the line that keeps the most also loses the least. In the example below the total is 36. The best line keeps 33 and loses 3.

examples.setup: Four students have maths and physics marks. After subtracting the average marks (the next card shows how), their positions are A $(-4,-2)$, B $(-1,1)$, C $(2,1)$, D $(3,0)$. You may keep only one number per student. Compare three lines: the maths axis, the physics axis, and a tilted line along $(3,1)$. Which keeps the most spread?
steps: Total squared distance from the centre: A $16+4=20$, B $1+1=2$, C $4+1=5$, D $9+0=9$. The total is $20+2+5+9=36$. No line can keep more than 36.
Maths axis: the shadows are the first coordinates $-4,-1,2,3$. Squares: $16+1+4+9=30$. Kept 30 of 36.
Physics axis: the shadows are $-2,1,1,0$. Squares: $4+1+1+0=6$. Kept only 6. B and C land on the same spot, so they look identical.

Tilted line, direction $u=(3,1)/\sqrt{10}$. The shadow is the dot product $(3x+y)/\sqrt{10}$. A: $-14/\sqrt{10}$, B: $-2/\sqrt{10}$, C: $7/\sqrt{10}$, D: $9/\sqrt{10}$. Squares: $(196+4+49+81)/10=330/10=33$.
Compare: 30, 6 and 33 out of 36. The tilted line keeps the most and loses only $36-33=3$. Dividing by $n-1=3$ turns these into variances 10, 2 and 11.
examples.answer: The tilted line along $(3,1)$ keeps 33 of the 36 units of spread (about 92%). That line is PC1. No labels were used anywhere.

examples.setup: Match each method to its job. Methods: (p) PCA, (q) k-means, (r) linear regression, (s) naive Bayes. Jobs: (i) group unlabelled points, (ii) predict a number from features, (iii) compress features without using labels, (iv) classify by modelling each class's feature distribution.
steps: For each method ask two questions: does it need labels, and what does it output?
PCA: no labels. Output: fewer coordinates per point. That is job (iii).
k-means: no labels. Output: a group number per point. That is job (i).
Linear regression: needs a numeric target. Output: a predicted number. That is job (ii).
Naive Bayes: needs class labels. It models $P(x\mid y)$ for each class. That is job (iv).
examples.answer: p-iii, q-i, r-ii, s-iv. PCA and k-means are both unsupervised. They differ in what they output: new coordinates versus group numbers.

examples.setup: Two classes sit at $(-4,2),(4,2)$ (red) and $(-4,-2),(4,-2)$ (blue). Is PC1 any use for telling the classes apart?
steps: The mean is $(0,0)$, so the data are already centred, and $n-1=3$.
Shadows on PC1: red $-4,4$; blue $-4,4$. The two classes land on exactly the same spots, so PC1 cannot separate them.
PC2 is the $x_2$ axis. Shadows: red $2,2$; blue $-2,-2$. PC2 separates the classes perfectly, yet it holds only $5.33/26.67=20\%$ of the variance.
examples.answer: PC1 is useless for the classes here. The useful direction is PC2, the low-variance one. PCA ignores labels, so it cannot know that.

cards.why: PCA compresses many features into a few, and it lets you draw high-dimensional data in 2D. It is the standard unsupervised dimensionality-reduction method. In GATE: place PCA among other methods, for example in a matching question.
how: Ask: does the method use labels? PCA does not.
Ask: what does it output? PCA outputs fewer coordinates per point, not a class and not a number.
Remember it is linear: each new feature is a weighted sum of the old ones.
For 'best direction' questions, maximum variance and minimum reconstruction error mean the same thing.
cards.mistake: Believing PC1 is the best direction for telling classes apart. PCA ignores labels and keeps spread only. Classes can differ along a low-variance direction, as the twist example shows. When labels exist and separation matters, use LDA.
edge_cases: Keeping all $d$ PCs loses nothing. It only rotates the axes.
$u$ and $-u$ are the same PC. The sign is arbitrary.
PCA is linear. A curved cloud (like a banana) cannot be captured exactly by one straight line.
A direction with large variance can still be pure noise. PCA cannot tell signal from noise.
connections: Linear algebra: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors. The PCs are eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (the next cards).
Linear algebra: Singular value decomposition gives the same PCs straight from the data table.
Linear discriminant analysis (another chapter) also projects onto a line, but it uses the labels to choose the line.
k-means clustering (another chapter) is the other unsupervised method in matching questions. It outputs groups, PCA outputs coordinates.
Foundations: Algebra covers the squares and sums used here.
Foundations: Functions and graphs covers reading points and lines on an x-y graph.

check.q: Does PCA use the class labels?
check.a: No. It is unsupervised: it uses only the features.

check.q: The squares of the shadows on a line add to 24. The squared distances of the points from the centre add to 30. How much spread is lost?
check.a: $30-24=6$. Kept plus lost equals the total.

check.q: True or false: the first PC always separates two classes best.
check.a: False. It maximises variance and ignores the labels.

cards.title: Centring and the covariance matrix
cards.simple: Imagine four students with maths and physics marks. Before looking for patterns, slide the whole picture so the average student sits in the middle of the page. That slide is centring: each mark minus the class average. Then write down how spread out the maths marks are, how spread out the physics marks are, and whether physics tends to go up when maths does. These facts go in a small square table called the covariance matrix. In exam words: subtract the mean of each feature, then $\Sigma=\frac1{n-1}X_c^\top X_c$. The diagonal holds the variances and the off-diagonal holds the covariances.
cards.idea: First slide the whole cloud so its average sits at the origin. This is **centring**: subtract each feature's mean from every value. Then build the **covariance matrix**, whose diagonal says how spread out each feature is and whose other entries say whether two features rise together.
cards.definition:
Centre each feature, then:

$$\Sigma=\frac1{n-1}X_c^\top X_c$$

Symbols: $X_c$ is the $n\times d$ table of centred data, one row per point. $\Sigma$ is a $d\times d$ matrix. Entry $\Sigma_{jj}$ is the variance of feature $j$: the sum of squares of its centred values, divided by $n-1$. Entry $\Sigma_{jk}$ is the covariance of features $j$ and $k$: the sum of (centred $j$) times (centred $k$), divided by $n-1$. $\Sigma$ is symmetric.
cards.intuition_full: Why centre? PCA looks for the direction in which points spread **around their centre**. If the cloud sits far from the origin, 'distance from the origin' mostly measures how far away the cloud is, so the first direction would just point at the cloud. After subtracting the mean, the origin is the middle of the data. Why a matrix? One variance per feature misses the tilt. A cloud that rises from lower left to upper right has positive covariance, and the matrix records it. The 3 in the example means students strong in maths tend to be strong in physics too. Why $n-1$? The mean was estimated from the same data, which uses up one degree of freedom. For PCA this barely matters: dividing by $n$ instead multiplies every entry by the same number, so eigenvalues scale while directions and variance ratios stay the same.

examples.setup: Four students have (maths, physics) marks A $(2,3)$, B $(5,6)$, C $(8,6)$, D $(9,5)$. Centre the data and find the covariance matrix.
steps: Squares of the maths column: $16+1+4+9=30$. Squares of the physics column: $4+1+1+0=6$.
Divide each sum by $n-1=3$. Variance of maths $=30/3=10$. Variance of physics $=6/3=2$. Covariance $=9/3=3$.
Write them as a matrix: variances on the diagonal, the covariance in both off-diagonal places.
examples.answer: $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}10&3\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$. The positive 3 says maths and physics marks rise together.

examples.setup: A dataset has $n=5$ centred points. Its scatter matrix is $X_c^\top X_c=\begin{pmatrix}40&24\\24&40\end{pmatrix}$. Find the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix with divisor $n-1$ and with divisor $n$. Do the principal directions or the explained-variance ratio change?
steps: Divisor $n-1=4$: $\Sigma=\frac14\begin{pmatrix}40&24\\24&40\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}10&6\\6&10\end{pmatrix}$.
Eigenvalues: trace $=20$, determinant $=100-36=64$. So $\lambda^2-20\lambda+64=0$, which factors as $(\lambda-16)(\lambda-4)=0$. The eigenvalues are 16 and 4.
Eigenvectors: for 16, $(10-16)v_1+6v_2=0$ gives $v_1=v_2$, so $(1,1)/\sqrt2$. For 4, $6v_1+6v_2=0$ gives $(1,-1)/\sqrt2$.
Divisor $n=5$: $\Sigma'=\frac15\begin{pmatrix}40&24\\24&40\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}8&4.8\\4.8&8\end{pmatrix}$. The eigenvalues are $8\pm4.8$: 12.8 and 3.2.
Same eigenvectors, $(1,1)/\sqrt2$ and $(1,-1)/\sqrt2$. Ratio of PC1: $16/20=0.8$ with divisor $n-1$ and $12.8/16=0.8$ with divisor $n$. Same.
examples.answer: Eigenvalues 16 and 4 (divisor $n-1$), or 12.8 and 3.2 (divisor $n$). The second set is the first multiplied by $4/5$. The directions and the 0.8 ratio do not change.

examples.setup: Three points $(20,1)$, $(20,3)$, $(20,5)$ have no spread at all in the first feature. Find the true PC1, then see what happens if you skip centring.
steps: $\Sigma$ with $n-1=2$: variance of feature 1 $=0$. Variance of feature 2 $=(4+0+4)/2=4$. Covariance $=0$. So $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&4\end{pmatrix}$ and PC1 $=(0,1)$ with variance 4. This is right: all the spread is in feature 2.
Its eigenvalues solve $\lambda^2-617.5\lambda+2400=0$, because $\det M=600\cdot17.5-90^2=10500-8100=2400$. They are about 613.6 and 3.9.
The top eigenvector solves $(600-613.6)v_1+90v_2=0$, so $v_2=0.151\,v_1$. Normalised, it is about $(0.989,\ 0.149)$. That is the direction of the mean $(20,3)$, not of the spread.
examples.answer: Without centring, 'PC1' is $(0.99,\,0.15)$ with 'variance' 613.6. It points at where the data sit. The true PC1 is $(0,1)$ with variance 4.

cards.why: Every PCA problem starts with the covariance matrix. If you centre wrongly or divide wrongly, every later number is off. In GATE: small tables where you build $\Sigma$ by hand, and statements about what the divisor changes.
how: Find the mean of each feature.
Subtract it from every value. Check that each column now adds to 0.
Variance: sum of squares of the column, divided by $n-1$.
Covariance: sum of products of two columns, divided by $n-1$.
Fill the symmetric matrix. Use the divisor the question states.
cards.mistake: Skipping the centring, or squaring raw values instead of centred ones. Then the first direction chases the position of the cloud instead of its spread. Always check that each centred column adds to 0 before you multiply.
edge_cases: Dividing by $n$ instead of $n-1$ multiplies every entry by the same number. Eigenvalues scale, but directions and ratios do not.
Two features that never move together have covariance 0, so $\Sigma$ is diagonal and the PCs are the original axes.
A feature that never changes has variance 0, so its row and column of $\Sigma$ are all zero.
$\Sigma$ is always symmetric, and its diagonal is never negative.

cards.title: Principal components as eigenvectors
cards.simple: Look at the cloud of dots again. Some directions through it are long and some are short, like a rugby ball seen from the side. The long direction is the first principal component. The short one at a right angle to it is the second. The table we built last time holds these directions: push an arrow along one of the special directions through the table and it comes out pointing the same way, only stretched. The stretch factor is exactly the spread of the dots along that direction. So finding the best directions means finding the table's special directions and their stretch factors. In exam words: the PCs are the eigenvectors of $\Sigma$ sorted by eigenvalue, and the variance along PC $k$ is $\lambda_k$.
cards.idea: A matrix usually turns an arrow, but for a few special arrows it only stretches them. The covariance matrix $\Sigma$ has such arrows, called **eigenvectors**, and the stretch factors are the **eigenvalues** $\lambda$. The eigenvector with the biggest $\lambda$ is the first principal component, PC1. The variance of the data along an eigenvector is exactly its eigenvalue.
cards.definition:
$$\Sigma\,u=\lambda\,u,\qquad \|u\|=1,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(u^\top x)=u^\top\Sigma\,u=\lambda$$

For a $2\times2$ matrix, the eigenvalues solve $\lambda^2-(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma)\,\lambda+\det\Sigma=0$.

Symbols: $u$ is a unit eigenvector and $\lambda$ its eigenvalue. $\operatorname{tr}$ is the sum of the diagonal. $\det$ is the determinant, $ad-bc$ for $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$. Sort $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots$ and PC $k$ is the eigenvector of $\lambda_k$. Different PCs are perpendicular because $\Sigma$ is symmetric.
cards.intuition_full: The variance of the shadows along a unit direction $u$ is $u^\top\Sigma u$. As $u$ turns, this number rises and falls, like the width of a rugby ball as you turn it. It is biggest along the long axis and smallest along the short axis. At those two directions $\Sigma u$ points the same way as $u$, so $\Sigma u=\lambda u$. That is why the extremes are eigenvectors. At such a $u$ the variance is $u^\top(\lambda u)=\lambda\,(u^\top u)=\lambda$. A second picture: the cloud looks like an ellipse, PC1 is its long axis and PC2 is its short axis. Because $\Sigma$ is symmetric, the two axes are perpendicular, so PC2 is the leftover direction at 90 degrees.

examples.setup: Find the principal components of the maths and physics data, whose covariance matrix from the last card is $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}10&3\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$.
steps: Trace and determinant. $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=10+2=12$. $\det\Sigma=10\cdot2-3\cdot3=20-9=11$.

Eigenvector for 11. $\Sigma-11I=\begin{pmatrix}-1&3\\3&-9\end{pmatrix}$. Row 1: $-v_1+3v_2=0$, so $v_1=3v_2$. Take $v=(3,1)$.
Make it a unit vector. Length $=\sqrt{3^2+1^2}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.162$. PC1 is $u_1=(3,1)/\sqrt{10}\approx(0.949,\ 0.316)$.
Eigenvector for 1. $\Sigma-I=\begin{pmatrix}9&3\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$. Row 1: $9v_1+3v_2=0$, so $v_2=-3v_1$. Take $v=(-1,3)$. PC2 is $u_2=(-1,3)/\sqrt{10}\approx(-0.316,\ 0.949)$.

examples.setup: A centred dataset in $\mathbb R^{30}$ has covariance eigenvalues $\lambda_i=2^{\,6-i}$ for $i=1,\dots,30$. Let $u$ be the unit direction of maximum variance. Find $\dfrac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\big(u^\top x^{(j)}\big)^2$.
steps: The data are centred, so the mean of the numbers $u^\top x^{(j)}$ is 0.
The average of the squares of numbers whose mean is 0 is their variance. So the quantity is $\operatorname{Var}(u^\top x)=u^\top\Sigma u$ (with divisor $n$, as the average in the question uses).
For the best unit direction, this is the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_1$.

examples.setup: For the same $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}10&3\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$, find the variance along the unit direction $u=(1,1)/\sqrt2$. Is this direction a PC?
steps: Variance $=u^\top\Sigma u=\dfrac{(1,1)}{\sqrt2}\cdot\dfrac{(13,5)}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{13+5}{2}=9$.
Sanity check: the variance along any unit direction lies between $\lambda_2=1$ and $\lambda_1=11$. And $9$ does.
A naive guess is to average the diagonal: $(10+2)/2=6$. That is wrong. The covariance adds $2\cdot3/2=3$, and $6+3=9$.
Not a PC: $\Sigma u=(13,5)/\sqrt2$ is not a multiple of $u$, because $13\ne5$.
examples.answer: The variance is 9. It lies between 1 and 11, and the direction is not a PC.

cards.what_full:
A matrix usually turns an arrow, but for a few special arrows it only stretches them. The covariance matrix $\Sigma$ has such arrows, called **eigenvectors**, and the stretch factors are the **eigenvalues** $\lambda$. The eigenvector with the biggest $\lambda$ is the first principal component, PC1. The variance of the data along an eigenvector is exactly its eigenvalue.

$$\Sigma\,u=\lambda\,u,\qquad \|u\|=1,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(u^\top x)=u^\top\Sigma\,u=\lambda$$

For a $2\times2$ matrix, the eigenvalues solve $\lambda^2-(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma)\,\lambda+\det\Sigma=0$.

Symbols: $u$ is a unit eigenvector and $\lambda$ its eigenvalue. $\operatorname{tr}$ is the sum of the diagonal. $\det$ is the determinant, $ad-bc$ for $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$. Sort $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots$ and PC $k$ is the eigenvector of $\lambda_k$. Different PCs are perpendicular because $\Sigma$ is symmetric.

**Worked example.** Find the principal components of the maths and physics data, whose covariance matrix from the last card is $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}10&3\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$.

1. Trace and determinant. $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=10+2=12$. $\det\Sigma=10\cdot2-3\cdot3=20-9=11$.
2. Characteristic equation: $\lambda^2-12\lambda+11=0$. Factor: $(\lambda-11)(\lambda-1)=0$. So $\lambda_1=11$ and $\lambda_2=1$. Check: $11+1=12$ and $11\cdot1=11$.
3. Eigenvector for 11. $\Sigma-11I=\begin{pmatrix}-1&3\\3&-9\end{pmatrix}$. Row 1: $-v_1+3v_2=0$, so $v_1=3v_2$. Take $v=(3,1)$.
4. Make it a unit vector. Length $=\sqrt{3^2+1^2}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.162$. PC1 is $u_1=(3,1)/\sqrt{10}\approx(0.949,\ 0.316)$.
5. Eigenvector for 1. $\Sigma-I=\begin{pmatrix}9&3\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$. Row 1: $9v_1+3v_2=0$, so $v_2=-3v_1$. Take $v=(-1,3)$. PC2 is $u_2=(-1,3)/\sqrt{10}\approx(-0.316,\ 0.949)$.
6. Check. Perpendicular: $3\cdot(-1)+1\cdot3=0$. Variance along PC1: $\Sigma(3,1)=(10\cdot3+3\cdot1,\ 3\cdot3+2\cdot1)=(33,11)=11\,(3,1)$, so $\Sigma u_1=11u_1$ and the variance is 11.

**Answer:** PC1 $=(3,1)/\sqrt{10}$ with variance 11. PC2 $=(-1,3)/\sqrt{10}$ with variance 1.

**Check yourself:** A $2\times2$ covariance matrix has trace 7 and determinant 6. Find the eigenvalues.

*Answer:* $\lambda^2-7\lambda+6=(\lambda-6)(\lambda-1)$, so 6 and 1.

cards.title: Explained variance ratio
cards.simple: Think of all the spread in the data as one pizza. PCA cuts the pizza into slices, one slice per direction. The first slice is the biggest, the next is smaller, and so on. How much of the pizza a slice takes is its explained variance ratio: slice divided by whole pizza. The size of the whole pizza is easy to find without any slices: add up the variances on the diagonal of the covariance table. If two slices already make up 90 percent of the pizza, you can throw the rest away and lose very little. In exam words: ratio $=\lambda_k/\sum\lambda_i$, and $\sum\lambda_i=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$.
cards.idea: The total spread in the data is shared out among the PCs. PC $k$ gets the share $\lambda_k$ over the total, called its **explained variance ratio**. The total is the sum of the diagonal of $\Sigma$ (the **trace**), which equals the sum of the eigenvalues. Keep the fewest PCs whose shares add up to enough.
cards.definition:
$$\text{ratio}_k=\frac{\lambda_k}{\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\dots+\lambda_d}=\frac{\lambda_k}{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma}$$

Symbols: $\lambda_k$ is the variance along PC $k$. $d$ is the number of features. $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$ is the sum of the diagonal entries of $\Sigma$. The cumulative ratio of the first $k$ PCs is $(\lambda_1+\dots+\lambda_k)/\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$.
cards.intuition_full: Turning the axes does not create or destroy spread. It only moves spread from one direction to another. So the total is the same before and after the turn. Before the turn, the total is the sum of the feature variances, which is the diagonal of $\Sigma$. After the turn, it is the sum of the eigenvalues. In the example, $10+2=11+1=12$. That is why $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=\sum\lambda_i$: the trace is the same in any set of perpendicular axes. In practice you never need all the eigenvalues to know the total. The shares are what you read off a scree plot, a bar chart of the eigenvalues. A steep drop means a few PCs carry the data, so compressing is cheap. A flat plot means every direction matters and compressing loses a lot.

examples.setup: From the last cards, $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}10&3\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues 11 and 1. Find the total variance, the explained variance ratio of each PC, and how many PCs you need to keep at least 90% of the variance.
steps: Total variance from the trace: $10+2=12$.
The eigenvalues give the same total: $11+1=12$. The axes turned, but the total did not change.
PC2: $1/12=0.0833$, which is 8.3%. The two ratios add up to 1.
Cumulative: after PC1 it is 0.9167, after PC2 it is 1. We need at least 0.90, so PC1 alone is enough.
examples.answer: The total is 12. The ratios are 0.9167 and 0.0833. One PC keeps 91.7% and meets the 90% target.

examples.setup: A covariance matrix has eigenvalues $10,\ 6,\ 3,\ 1$. What is the smallest number of PCs that keeps at least 90% of the variance? What is the ratio of PC2?
steps: The first cumulative value at or above 0.90 is $0.95$, after 3 PCs. With 2 PCs it is only 0.80.
examples.answer: Keep 3 PCs. The ratio of PC2 is 0.30.

examples.setup: Five features are standardised first (each then has variance 1), so the covariance matrix is the correlation matrix. Its two largest eigenvalues are 2.5 and 1.3. Find the ratios of PC1 and PC2 without knowing the other three eigenvalues.
steps: Each standardised feature has variance 1, so the diagonal of $\Sigma$ is five 1s.
Trace $=1+1+1+1+1=5$. So the total variance is 5.
The other three eigenvalues must add up to $5-2.5-1.3=1.2$. We never needed them individually.
examples.answer: PC1 explains 50% and PC2 explains 26%. For standardised data the total variance equals the number of features.

cards.why: The ratio tells you how much information a short version keeps. It is how you decide how many PCs to retain. In GATE: the fraction explained by PC1 from given eigenvalues, or the fewest PCs for a target such as 90%.
how: Find the total: add all the eigenvalues, or add the diagonal of $\Sigma$ (the trace).
Divide each eigenvalue by that total.
Add the ratios from the top to get the cumulative ratio.
Stop at the first number of PCs whose cumulative ratio reaches the target.
cards.mistake: Dividing by $\lambda_1$ instead of by the total. That gives a number above 1 for the other PCs, which should warn you. Another slip is using only the first two eigenvalues as the total. The denominator is the sum of **all** the eigenvalues.
edge_cases: The ratios always add up to 1. The cumulative ratio of all $d$ PCs is exactly 1.
Equal eigenvalues (spherical data) give each PC the share $1/d$.
Standardised data have total variance $d$, because the diagonal is all 1s.
An eigenvalue of 0 gives a ratio of 0. That direction carries nothing.
connections: Linear algebra: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors covers the fact that the sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace.
Foundations: Algebra covers fractions and percentages.
Previous card: the eigenvalues. Next card: using the PCs to compress one point.
The bend in a scree plot works like the elbow in k-means clustering (another chapter): pick where the curve flattens.

cards.title: Projection and reconstruction
cards.simple: Take one student's dot on the page. To describe it with one number, start at the class average, walk along the stick and drop straight down onto it. How far you walked is the score: one number for that student. To get a picture of the student back, go from the average the same distance along the stick. You land near the original dot, but not exactly on it. The gap between where you land and the real dot is what you lost. The lost part is exactly the spread along the directions you threw away. In exam words: score $z=u^\top(x-\mu)$, rebuilt point $\hat x=\mu+zu$, and the mean squared error is the sum of the dropped eigenvalues.
cards.idea: To compress a point, centre it and take its **score**: the dot product with the PC. The score is one number, the distance of the point's shadow from the mean along the PC. To rebuild the point, walk from the mean by the score along the PC. The rebuilt point is the **reconstruction**, and what is lost is the part perpendicular to the PC.
cards.definition:
$$z=u^\top(x-\mu),\qquad \hat x=\mu+z\,u,\qquad \text{error}=\|x-\hat x\|^2$$

Symbols: $x$ is a data point, $\mu$ the mean, $u$ a unit PC, $z$ the score (a single number), and $\hat x$ (read 'x hat') the reconstruction. With $k$ PCs: $z_j=u_j^\top(x-\mu)$ and $\hat x=\mu+\sum_{j\le k}z_ju_j$. Averaged over the data, the squared error is $\sum_{i>k}\lambda_i$: the eigenvalues you dropped.
cards.intuition_full: Drop a ball straight onto a wall. The spot where it lands is its shadow. The drop is at 90 degrees to the wall, so there is a right triangle: the centred point is the long side, the score is one short side, and the error is the other. So (centred length)$^2$ = $z^2$ + error$^2$. When we keep only PC1, the error of a point is its PC2 score, and its squared error is the PC2 score squared. Average that over the data: the average of squared PC2 scores is the variance along PC2, which is $\lambda_2$. That is why the error with $k$ PCs kept is the sum of the dropped eigenvalues. PC1 is the best line because it leaves the smallest leftover.

examples.setup: Use the maths and physics data. The mean is $\mu=(6,5)$ and PC1 is $u_1=(3,1)/\sqrt{10}$. Compress student D $=(9,5)$ to one number, rebuild it, and measure what is lost.
steps: All four students: the squared PC2 scores are $0.4,\ 1.6,\ 0.1,\ 0.9$ (A, B, C, D). They add to $3.0$. Divide by $n-1=3$: the mean squared error is $1=\lambda_2$.
examples.answer: Score 2.846, reconstruction $(8.7,\,5.9)$, squared error 0.90. Over all the students the mean squared error is 1, the dropped eigenvalue $\lambda_2$.

examples.setup: A covariance matrix has eigenvalues $9,\ 5,\ 3,\ 1$. A dataset is compressed by keeping the top 2 PCs. Find the expected mean squared reconstruction error per point, and the fraction of the variance that is lost.
steps: The error is the sum of the dropped eigenvalues, the ones for PC3 and PC4.
Total variance $=9+5+3+1=18$.
Fraction lost $=4/18=0.222$. Fraction kept $=14/18=0.778$.
Trap: the error is **not** $9+5=14$. That is the part kept.
examples.answer: The mean squared error is 4. About 22.2% of the variance is lost.

examples.setup: A student wrongly uses $v=(3,1)$ (not normalised) as if it were the PC. Show what goes wrong for D $=(9,5)$, then fix it.
steps: Centred D: $(3,0)$.
Wrong score: $v\cdot(3,0)=9$, instead of 2.846.
Wrong rebuild: $\mu+9\,v=(6,5)+(27,9)=(33,14)$. That is far from D $=(9,5)$.
Fix: divide by $v\cdot v=10$. Rebuild $=\mu+\dfrac{v\cdot(3,0)}{v\cdot v}\,v=(6,5)+\dfrac{9}{10}(3,1)=(8.7,\ 5.9)$.
That matches the correct answer.
examples.answer: Always normalise $u$ first, or divide by $v\cdot v$. Skipping this makes the score $\sqrt{10}$ times too big and the step away from the mean 10 times too long.

cards.why: Projection is how PCA compresses: each point becomes a few scores. Reconstruction shows what was lost. In GATE: the score of a point on a given PC, and the reconstruction error from the eigenvalues.
how: Subtract the mean: $x-\mu$.
Check that $u$ has length 1. If not, divide it by its length.
Score: $z=u\cdot(x-\mu)$.
Rebuild: $\hat x=\mu+zu$. Do not forget to add $\mu$ back.
The mean squared error with $k$ PCs kept is the sum of the dropped eigenvalues.
cards.mistake: Forgetting to normalise $u$, or forgetting to subtract (or add back) the mean. An unnormalised $u$ inflates the score. Without the mean, the score is measured from the origin and the rebuilt point lands far from the cloud.
edge_cases: Keeping all $d$ PCs gives $\hat x=x$ exactly. The error is 0.
Keeping 0 PCs gives $\hat x=\mu$ for every point. The error is the total variance.
A point that already lies on the PC line has error 0.
Scores can be negative. The sign only says which side of the mean the point is on.

cards.title: PCA and SVD
cards.simple: There are two ways to find the best directions: build the table of spreads as we did, or skip the table and run a standard recipe called SVD on the data directly. The SVD splits the data table into three simple pieces: a turn, a stretch and another turn. The stretch numbers, called singular values, tell you how big each direction is. Square a singular value and divide by one less than the number of points to get the spread along that direction. The directions themselves come out as the last turn. In exam words: for centred $X_c=USV^\top$, the PCs are the columns of $V$, $\lambda_i=\sigma_i^2/(n-1)$, and the scores are $X_cV=US$.
cards.idea: The SVD splits the centred data table $X_c$ into a turn, a stretch and a turn. The last turn, $V$, holds the principal components, and the stretch numbers $\sigma_i$ are the **singular values**. Square one and divide by $n-1$ to get the variance along that PC, with no need to form $\Sigma$.
cards.definition:
$$X_c=U\,S\,V^\top,\qquad \lambda_i=\frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1},\qquad \text{scores}=X_cV=US$$

Symbols: $X_c$ is the centred $n\times d$ table. $U$ ($n\times d$) and $V$ ($d\times d$) have perpendicular unit columns. $S$ is diagonal and holds the singular values $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\dots\ge0$. (Many books write $\Sigma$ for $S$. Here we use $S$ so it does not clash with the covariance matrix.) The columns of $V$ are the PCs. Each row of the scores is one point's coordinates along the PC axes.
cards.intuition_full: The covariance matrix is $\Sigma=X_c^\top X_c/(n-1)$. Put in $X_c=USV^\top$: $X_c^\top X_c=VS\,U^\top U\,SV^\top=VS^2V^\top$, because $U^\top U=I$. That is an eigen-decomposition of $X_c^\top X_c$, with eigenvectors $V$ and eigenvalues $\sigma_i^2$. So the PCs are the columns of $V$, and the covariance eigenvalues are $\sigma_i^2/(n-1)$. Squares appear because $X_c^\top X_c$ multiplies the data by itself. The scores $X_cV=USV^\top V=US$ have perpendicular columns of lengths $\sigma_i$. Perpendicular columns of centred scores mean that scores on different PCs are uncorrelated. In practice, a computer finds the SVD more accurately than it forms and solves $\Sigma$.

examples.setup: The centred maths and physics table is $X_c=\begin{pmatrix}-4&-2\\-1&1\\2&1\\3&0\end{pmatrix}$ ($n-1=3$). Get the PCs, the variances and the scores by the SVD route.
steps: Form $X_c^\top X_c$. The squares and products are $30,\ 6,\ 9$ (from the covariance card), so $X_c^\top X_c=\begin{pmatrix}30&9\\9&6\end{pmatrix}$. Its eigenvalues: trace $36$, determinant $30\cdot6-81=99$, so $\lambda^2-36\lambda+99=(\lambda-33)(\lambda-3)=0$. Hence $\sigma_1^2=33$ and $\sigma_2^2=3$.

Singular values: $\sigma_1=\sqrt{33}\approx5.745$ and $\sigma_2=\sqrt3\approx1.732$. Variances: $\sigma_1^2/(n-1)=33/3=11$ and $\sigma_2^2/(n-1)=3/3=1$. These are the eigenvalues of $\Sigma$ from before.
$V$: the eigenvectors of $X_c^\top X_c$ are the same as those of $\Sigma$, namely $u_1=(3,1)/\sqrt{10}$ and $u_2=(-1,3)/\sqrt{10}$.

Check: the squares of column 1 add to $(196+4+49+81)/10=33=\sigma_1^2$. The squares of column 2 add to $(4+16+1+9)/10=3=\sigma_2^2$. The columns multiply to $(28-8+7-27)/10=0$, so the scores are uncorrelated.
examples.answer: PCs $(3,1)/\sqrt{10}$ and $(-1,3)/\sqrt{10}$. Variances 11 and 1. Singular values $5.745$ and $1.732$. The two score columns are perpendicular, with lengths $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$.

examples.setup: A centred data matrix $X_c$ has $n=11$ rows and singular values $10,\ 6,\ 2$. Find the variance along PC1 and the explained ratio of PC1. Also show what the mistake of using $\sigma$ instead of $\sigma^2$ would give.
steps: Variances $\lambda_i=\sigma_i^2/10$: $10,\ 3.6,\ 0.4$. Check: they add to $14=140/10$.

examples.answer: $\lambda_1=10$, and PC1 explains $5/7\approx0.714$.

steps: Ratio of PC1: $9.09/12.73=0.714$. The same.

cards.title: Spherical data and tied eigenvalues
cards.simple: Suppose the dots are spread equally in every direction, like a round puddle. There is no long side and no short side. Any stick you lay across it gives the same spread. So PCA has no favourite: you can pick any stick for the first direction, and any stick at a right angle to it for the second. A smaller version happens when only two directions have exactly the same spread. Then you can pick any right-angle pair of sticks inside that flat patch, while the other directions stay fixed. In exam words: if $\Sigma=cI$, every orthonormal basis is a valid set of PCs. When some eigenvalues tie, only the PCs inside the tied eigenspace are free.
cards.idea: If the data are spread equally in all directions, they are called **spherical**, and nothing singles out one direction. Then $\Sigma=cI$, every eigenvalue is the same, and every direction has the same variance. Any pair of perpendicular directions is a valid set of PCs. A smaller version of this freedom appears when only some eigenvalues tie.
cards.definition:
$$\Sigma=c\,I\ \Longrightarrow\ u^\top\Sigma u=c\,(u^\top u)=c\quad\text{for every unit vector }u$$

Symbols: $c>0$ is the common variance and $I$ is the identity matrix. Every non-zero vector satisfies $\Sigma v=cv$, so every non-zero vector is an eigenvector. A valid set of PCs is then any set of non-zero, mutually perpendicular directions. 'Orthogonal' means perpendicular. 'Orthonormal' also means unit length, but PCs are directions, so length does not matter. Each PC explains $1/d$ of the variance. If only some eigenvalues tie, PCs for the **different** eigenvalues are fixed (up to sign), while those sharing a value can be any perpendicular set inside their shared plane.
cards.intuition_full: PCA asks for the direction with the biggest variance. When all directions tie, the question has no single answer, like asking for the tallest in a class where everyone is the same height. Every choice is a correct answer. In algebra, $(\Sigma-cI)v=0$ holds for every $v$, so the eigenspace is the whole space. In 3 dimensions with eigenvalues 9, 4, 4, there is one tall direction and a round, flat disc around it. The tall direction is fixed. The disc is round, so any two perpendicular directions in the disc are equally good. This freedom is why exams ask 'which pairs can be PCs': you only check that each pair is perpendicular and non-zero.

examples.setup: Four centred points: $(3,0),\ (0,3),\ (-3,0),\ (0,-3)$. Find $\Sigma$ and show that every direction has the same variance.
steps: The mean is $(0,0)$, so the data are centred, and $n-1=3$. Variance of feature 1: $(9+0+9+0)/3=6$. Feature 2: $(0+9+0+9)/3=6$. Covariance: $\big(3\cdot0+0\cdot3+(-3)\cdot0+0\cdot(-3)\big)/3=0$. So $\Sigma=6I$.
Eigenvalues: $(\lambda-6)^2=0$, so $\lambda=6$ twice. They tie.
Test $u=(1,0)$. Shadows: $3,\ 0,\ -3,\ 0$. Squares add to $18$. Variance $18/3=6$.
PC2 only has to be perpendicular to PC1, for example $(-0.8,\ 0.6)$, since $0.6(-0.8)+0.8(0.6)=0$.
Turn the pair to $45^\circ$: $u=(0.707,\ 0.707)$ gives shadows $\pm2.12$, squares $4\times4.5=18$, variance $18/3=6$. So PC1 can be any unit vector, and PC2 any unit vector perpendicular to it.
examples.answer: $\Sigma=6I$. Every direction has variance 6, so any perpendicular pair is a valid set of PCs. Each PC explains 50%.

examples.setup: The data are spherical with $\Sigma=5I$ in $\mathbb R^2$. Which pairs of directions can be the two PCs? (i) $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$; (ii) $(2,1)$ and $(1,2)$; (iii) $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$; (iv) $(3,-4)$ and $(4,3)$.
steps: $\Sigma=5I$ is spherical, so all directions tie. Any perpendicular pair of non-zero vectors works.
(i) $1\cdot1+1\cdot(-1)=0$. Perpendicular.
(ii) $2\cdot1+1\cdot2=4\ne0$. Not perpendicular.
(iii) $1\cdot0+0\cdot1=0$. Perpendicular.
(iv) $3\cdot4+(-4)\cdot3=12-12=0$. Perpendicular.
Lengths do not matter. $(1,1)$ and $(3,-4)$ are not unit vectors, but only the direction counts.
examples.answer: (i), (iii) and (iv).

PC2 and PC3 share the eigenvalue 4. Their eigenspace is the $x_2$-$x_3$ plane: every vector $(0,a,b)$.

examples.answer: PC1 is fixed. PC2 and PC3 can be any perpendicular pair in the $x_2$-$x_3$ plane. The ratios are the same either way.

cards.title: Scale matters: standardise first
cards.simple: Suppose a shop records each apple's weight in kilograms and its width in metres. The weights vary by whole kilograms, but the widths vary by a few centimetres, which is a tiny number of metres. Ask 'which feature varies more?' and the answer depends on the units, not on the apples. PCA does exactly this: it only looks at the size of the numbers, so the feature with the biggest numbers grabs the first PC. Change kilograms to grams and the winner changes. The cure is to divide each feature by its own spread first, so every feature starts on equal footing. In exam words: PCA is not scale-invariant. Standardise the features (mean 0, variance 1) before PCA when units differ.
cards.idea: PCA measures spread in whatever units your numbers use. A feature measured in small units has big numbers and a big variance, so it grabs PC1, even though nothing real changed. This is why PCA is **not scale-invariant**. When features have different units, **standardise** them first: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation.
cards.definition:
$$z=\frac{x-\mu}{s}\ \ (\text{for each feature}),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(c\,x)=c^2\operatorname{Var}(x)$$

Symbols: $s$ is the standard deviation of that feature (the square root of its variance). $c$ is a scale factor, such as 100 for metres to centimetres. After standardising, every feature has variance 1, so $\Sigma$ becomes the **correlation matrix** $R$, which has 1s on the diagonal. For 2 features with correlation $r$, $R=\begin{pmatrix}1&r\\r&1\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $1+r$ and $1-r$.
cards.intuition_full: Multiply a feature by $c$ and every value stretches by $c$, so the variance stretches by $c^2$. A feature stretched by 10 has a variance 100 times larger, so its direction dominates. PCA has no idea that the stretch was only a change of units, because it only sees numbers. Standardising removes the units: dividing by $s$ gives variance $s^2/s^2=1$, whatever the original units were. Then the PCs reflect the **pattern of correlation**, not the units. There is a trade-off. If you want features with a large natural spread to count more, you would not standardise. Use standardised PCA when units differ, and raw PCA when all features share the same unit (pixel brightness, say).

examples.setup: Five centred points $(x_1,x_2)$: $(4,0),\ (-4,0),\ (0,2),\ (0,-2),\ (0,0)$. Find $\Sigma$ and PC1. Then change the unit of feature 2 so that every value triples, and redo it. Finally standardise.
steps: Original, with $n-1=4$. Variance of $x_1$: $(16+16)/4=8$. Variance of $x_2$: $(4+4)/4=2$. Covariance 0. So $\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(8,2)$. PC1 is the $x_1$ axis, with ratio $8/10=0.80$.
Triple feature 2: its values become $\pm6$ and $0$. Its variance is $(36+36)/4=18$. So $\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(8,18)$. The variance grew $3^2=9$ times: $2\times9=18$.
Now PC1 is the $x_2$ axis, with ratio $18/26=0.692$. Same students, same facts, but PC1 flipped.
Standardise instead. Divide $x_1$ by $\sqrt8$ and $x_2$ by $\sqrt{18}$ (after tripling; before tripling you would divide by $\sqrt2$). Both variances become $8/8=1$ and $18/18=1$.
Now $\Sigma=I$ in both unit systems. The PCs tie and each ratio is $0.5$. The unit change no longer matters.
examples.answer: Raw PCA: PC1 flips from $x_1$ (ratio 0.80) to $x_2$ (ratio 0.692) just because of units. After standardising, the answer is the same whatever the units.

examples.setup: The weight (kg) and height (m) of students are uncorrelated, with variances 25 and 0.04. (a) Find the ratio of PC1 and say which feature it is. (b) Height is converted to centimetres, so its variance becomes 400. Redo it. (c) Standardise.
steps: (b) Height in cm: $100^2\times0.04=400$. Total $=25+400=425$. PC1 is now height. Ratio $400/425=0.9412$.
The same students gave two different PC1s. The units decided, not the students.
(c) Standardised: both variances are 1 and the features are uncorrelated, so $\Sigma=I$. Each ratio is $1/2=0.5$ in both unit systems.
examples.answer: (a) 0.9984, weight. (b) 0.9412, height. (c) 0.5 each. PCA is not scale-invariant, and standardising fixes it.

examples.setup: Two standardised features have correlation $r=0.6$. Find the PCs and the explained ratios.
steps: Standardised, so $\Sigma=R=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.6\\0.6&1\end{pmatrix}$.
Trace $=2$, determinant $=1-0.36=0.64$. So $\lambda^2-2\lambda+0.64=0$, and $\lambda=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4-2.56}}{2}=\dfrac{2\pm1.2}{2}$, which gives $1.6$ and $0.4$. (Shortcut: $1\pm r$.)
examples.answer: PC1 $=(1,1)/\sqrt2$ with ratio 0.8. PC2 $=(1,-1)/\sqrt2$ with ratio 0.2.

cards.what: PCA measures spread in whatever units your numbers use. A feature measured in small units has big numbers and a big variance, so it grabs PC1, even though nothing real changed. This is why PCA is **not scale-invariant**. When features have different units, **standardise** them first: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation.

$$z=\frac{x-\mu}{s}\ \ (\text{for each feature}),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(c\,x)=c^2\operatorname{Var}(x)$$

Symbols: $s$ is the standard deviation of that feature (the square root of its variance). $c$ is a scale factor, such as 100 for metres to centimetres. After standardising, every feature has variance 1, so $\Sigma$ becomes the **correlation matrix** $R$, which has 1s on the diagonal. For 2 features with correlation $r$, $R=\begin{pmatrix}1&r\\r&1\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $1+r$ and $1-r$.

**Worked example.** Five centred points $(x_1,x_2)$: $(4,0),\ (-4,0),\ (0,2),\ (0,-2),\ (0,0)$. Find $\Sigma$ and PC1. Then change the unit of feature 2 so that every value triples, and redo it. Finally standardise.

2. Triple feature 2: its values become $\pm6$ and $0$. Its variance is $(36+36)/4=18$. So $\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(8,18)$. The variance grew $3^2=9$ times: $2\times9=18$.
3. Now PC1 is the $x_2$ axis, with ratio $18/26=0.692$. Same students, same facts, but PC1 flipped.
4. Standardise instead. Divide $x_1$ by $\sqrt8$ and $x_2$ by $\sqrt{18}$ (after tripling; before tripling you would divide by $\sqrt2$). Both variances become $8/8=1$ and $18/18=1$.

cards.title: Rank limit of the covariance matrix
cards.simple: Imagine two dots in a big room. Draw a line through them. All the spread of those dots lies along that one line, however big the room is. In general, $n$ dots can spread in at most $n-1$ independent directions. The reason: once you slide the middle of the dots to the origin, the last dot is forced by the others. The data may have 1000 features, but with only 10 dots just 9 directions can have any spread, and all the other directions have a spread of exactly zero. In exam words: the sample covariance has rank at most $\min(n-1,d)$, so it has at most that many non-zero eigenvalues.
cards.idea: After centring, the $n$ rows of the data add up to the zero vector. So one row is fixed by the others, and there are at most $n-1$ independent directions. The covariance matrix therefore has at most $\min(n-1,\,d)$ non-zero eigenvalues. Every other eigenvalue is exactly 0.
cards.definition:
$$\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma)\le\min(n-1,\ d)$$

Symbols: $n$ is the number of points and $d$ the number of features. Rank is the number of independent directions, which is also the number of non-zero eigenvalues of $\Sigma$. The bound can be lower still if the features are exactly dependent, for example $x_3=x_1+x_2$.
cards.intuition_full: Take the centred table $X_c$. Adding all its rows gives the zero vector, because every column has mean 0. So any one row equals minus the sum of the others. That removes one independent row, and the rank of $X_c$ is at most $n-1$. Also, a table with $d$ columns has rank at most $d$. And $\Sigma=X_c^\top X_c/(n-1)$ has the same rank as $X_c$. A picture: $n$ points always fit inside a flat space of dimension $n-1$ (2 points on a line, 3 points on a plane, 4 points in a 3D space). The data cannot spread outside it, so the directions outside have variance 0. This matters when you have few samples and many features, such as 50 patients and 20,000 genes: PCA can find at most 49 PCs with any variance.

examples.setup: Two points in three features: $P=(1,2,3)$ and $Q=(3,0,5)$. Find $\Sigma$ (divisor $n-1=1$) and count its non-zero eigenvalues.
steps: Centre: $P-\mu=(-1,\ 1,\ -1)$ and $Q-\mu=(1,\ -1,\ 1)$. The two rows add to $(0,0,0)$.
$X_c=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1&-1\\1&-1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Row 2 is $-1$ times row 1, so the rank is 1.
$\Sigma=X_c^\top X_c/1$. Every entry is $\pm2$: for example $(-1)(-1)+(1)(1)=2$ and $(-1)(1)+(1)(-1)=-2$. So $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&-2&2\\-2&2&-2\\2&-2&2\end{pmatrix}$.
Trace $=2+2+2=6$. With rank 1 there is only one non-zero eigenvalue, so $\lambda_1=6$ and $\lambda_2=\lambda_3=0$.
PC1 is the direction of $P-Q$: $(-1,1,-1)/\sqrt3$. The line through the two points holds all the spread there is.
examples.answer: Rank 1, with eigenvalues $6,\ 0,\ 0$. With $n=2$ points the bound $\min(n-1,d)=\min(1,3)=1$ is reached.

examples.setup: (a) A dataset has $n=8$ points and $d=20$ features. (b) Another has $n=50$ points and $d=6$ features. What is the maximum number of non-zero eigenvalues of the sample covariance in each case?
steps: Use $\min(n-1,\ d)$.
In (a) there are fewer points than features, so the points limit the rank. In (b) there are plenty of points, so the features limit it.

examples.setup: Three features obey $x_3=x_1+x_2$ exactly, and a very large sample gives $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&2\\0&3&3\\2&3&5\end{pmatrix}$. How many non-zero eigenvalues are there, and what are they?
steps: The sample size does not help here: $n-1$ is huge. But $x_3$ carries no new information, so the rank is at most 2.
Find the zero direction. Try $v=(1,1,-1)$: $\Sigma v=(2+0-2,\ 0+3-3,\ 2+3-5)=(0,0,0)$. So 0 is an eigenvalue.
Trace $=2+3+5=10$. The other two eigenvalues add up to 10.
Their product equals the sum of the three $2\times2$ principal minors (for eigenvalues $a,b,0$ that sum is $ab$): $(2\cdot3-0)+(2\cdot5-4)+(3\cdot5-9)=6+6+6=18$.
So $\lambda^2-10\lambda+18=0$, which gives $\lambda=5\pm\sqrt7\approx7.646$ and $2.354$.
examples.answer: Two non-zero eigenvalues, $5\pm\sqrt7$, and one zero. An exact dependence among features lowers the rank below the $\min(n-1,d)$ bound.

cards.why: It explains why PCA on a few samples with many features gives zero variance in most directions. In GATE: the maximum number of non-zero eigenvalues, given $n$ and $d$.
how: Write down $n$ and $d$.
Compute $\min(n-1,\ d)$. That is the maximum number of non-zero eigenvalues.
Check whether any feature is an exact combination of the others. If so, subtract 1 for each such dependency.
The number of non-zero eigenvalues is the rank of $\Sigma$.
cards.mistake: Using $\min(n,d)$ instead of $\min(n-1,d)$. Centring uses up one dimension. Eight points in 20 features give at most 7 non-zero eigenvalues, not 8.
edge_cases: $n=1$: a single point has no spread, and the covariance matrix is all zeros (rank 0).
When $n-1<d$, the zero eigenvalues make $\Sigma$ singular (not invertible).
The bound is an upper bound. Exact dependencies among features lower the rank.
Without centring, the bound would be $\min(n,d)$. Centring costs one.
connections: Linear algebra: Systems of equations and rank covers rank, including the rank of $X^\top X$.
Linear algebra: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors covers the fact that a symmetric matrix has as many non-zero eigenvalues as its rank.
Linear algebra: Singular value decomposition covers the fact that the number of non-zero singular values is the rank.
Foundations: Algebra covers the min of two numbers and simple counting.
Linear discriminant analysis (another chapter) has a similar limit: at most $C-1$ non-zero eigenvalues for $C$ classes.

scenes.title: Which line keeps the most spread?

steps.caption: Four students, centred marks. Squared distances from the centre: $16+4$, $1+1$, $4+1$, $9+0$. The total is $20+2+5+9=36$. No line can keep more than that.
Keep only maths: drop each point straight down onto the maths axis. Shadows $-4,-1,2,3$ have squares $16+1+4+9=30$. Kept 30 of 36.
Keep only physics: shadows $-2,1,1,0$ give $4+1+1+0=6$. B and C land on the same spot, so they now look identical. Kept 6.
Tilt the line along $(3,1)$. Each shadow is $(3x+y)/\sqrt{10}$, which gives $-14,-2,7,9$ over $\sqrt{10}$. The squares add to $330/10=33$. Kept 33.
30, 6 and 33 out of 36. The tilted line keeps the most and loses only 3. That line is PC1. No labels were used anywhere.
Four students. The mean maths mark is $(2+5+8+9)/4=6$ and the mean physics mark is $(3+6+6+5)/4=5$. The ring marks the mean $(6,5)$.
Subtract the mean from every point. The cloud slides so the mean sits at the origin. Centred points: $(-4,-2)$, $(-1,1)$, $(2,1)$, $(3,0)$. Each column adds to 0.
Square each centred value and add up. Maths: $16+1+4+9=30$. Physics: $4+1+1+0=6$.
Multiply the two centred values of each student and add up: $8,-1,2,0$ give $9$.
Divide each sum by $n-1=3$. Variance of maths $30/3=10$, variance of physics $6/3=2$, covariance $9/3=3$.
Put them in a matrix. The positive 3 says students strong in maths tend to be strong in physics.

scenes.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the covariance matrix

steps.caption: The covariance matrix from the last card. Trace $=10+2=12$. Determinant $=10\times2-3\times3=20-9=11$.
Solve the characteristic equation. It factors as $(\lambda-11)(\lambda-1)=0$, so the variances along the two PCs are 11 and 1.
Eigenvector for 11. Row 1 of $\Sigma-11I$ says $-v_1+3v_2=0$, so $v_1=3v_2$. Take $v=(3,1)$. It points along the stretch of the cloud.
Divide by the length $\sqrt{3^2+1^2}=\sqrt{10}=3.162$. The arrow shrinks to length 1: PC1 is $u_1=(0.949,\,0.316)$.
Eigenvector for 1. Row 1 of $\Sigma-I$ says $9v_1+3v_2=0$, so $v_2=-3v_1$. Take $v=(-1,3)$ and divide by $\sqrt{10}$: PC2 is $u_2=(-0.316,\,0.949)$.
Check: $3\cdot(-1)+1\cdot3=0$, so the PCs are at 90 degrees. The variance along PC1 is 11 because $\Sigma(3,1)=(33,11)=11\,(3,1)$.
The total variance is the sum of the diagonal of $\Sigma$ (the trace): $10+2=12$. The whole bar below is 12 units long.
Turn to the PC axes. The eigenvalues are 11 and 1, and $11+1=12$. Turning the axes moves variance around but the total stays the same.
Explained variance ratio of PC1 is its eigenvalue over the total: $11/12=0.9167$, about 91.7%.
PC2: $1/12=0.0833$, about 8.3%. The two ratios add up to 1.
Target: keep at least 90%. PC1 alone reaches 0.9167, past the dashed 90% mark, so one PC is enough.

scenes.title: Project a point on PC1 and rebuild it

steps.caption: Student D $=(9,5)$. Subtract the mean $(6,5)$: the centred point is $(3,0)$. The arrow runs from the mean to D.
The score is the dot product with $u_1=(3,1)/\sqrt{10}$: $(3\cdot3+1\cdot0)/\sqrt{10}=9/3.162=2.846$. It is the length of D's shadow along PC1.
Rebuild: $z\,u_1=\tfrac{9}{10}(3,1)=(2.7,\,0.9)$. Add the mean back: $(6,5)+(2.7,0.9)=(8.7,\,5.9)$. That is $\hat x$, the foot of the shadow.
The error vector runs from $\hat x$ to D: $(9-8.7,\ 5-5.9)=(0.3,\,-0.9)$. Squared error $=0.09+0.81=0.90$.
Check with PC2 $=(-1,3)/\sqrt{10}$. D's PC2 score is $-3/\sqrt{10}=-0.949$, and $0.949^2=0.90$. The error is exactly the PC2 part of D.
Do all four students. Squared errors are $0.4,\,1.6,\,0.1,\,0.9$ for A, B, C, D and they add to $3.0$. Divide by $n-1=3$: mean squared error $1=\lambda_2$.

scenes.title: PCA from the SVD of the centred table

steps.caption: Stack the centred points as the rows of $X$. Then $X^\top X=\begin{pmatrix}30&9\\9&6\end{pmatrix}$. Its eigenvalues solve $\lambda^2-36\lambda+99=(\lambda-33)(\lambda-3)=0$. These are $\sigma^2$: 33 and 3.
Singular values: $\sigma_1=\sqrt{33}=5.745$ and $\sigma_2=\sqrt3=1.732$. Divide $\sigma^2$ by $n-1=3$ and the bars shrink three times, to the variances 11 and 1.
The columns of $V$ are the PCs: $u_1=(0.949,\,0.316)$ and $u_2=(-0.316,\,0.949)$, the same eigenvectors as before.
Scores are X times V. Each student's row is multiplied by the PCs: the first column is the position along PC1, the second along PC2.
The squares in each score column add to $\sigma^2$ (33 and 3). The two columns multiply to $(28-8+7-27)/10=0$, so scores on different PCs are uncorrelated.
Four centred points on a circle (mean $(0,0)$, $n-1=3$). Variance of $x_1$: $(9+0+9+0)/3=6$. Variance of $x_2$: $6$. Covariance: $0$. So $\Sigma=6I$, the same number in every direction.
The eigenvalues are 6 and 6: a tie. Both PCs have the same variance, so no direction beats another.
Try $u=(1,0)$. The shadows $3,0,-3,0$ have squares adding to $18$, and $18/3=6$.
PC2 only needs to be at 90 degrees to PC1. $(-0.8,\,0.6)$ works because $0.6(-0.8)+0.8(0.6)=0$.
Turn the pair again, to 45 degrees: $u=(0.707,\,0.707)$ gives shadows $\pm2.12$, squares $4\times4.5=18$, variance 6 again. Any pair of perpendicular directions is a valid set of PCs.

scenes.title: Change the units and PC1 flips

steps.caption: Five centred points. $x_1$ takes values $\pm4$: variance $32/4=8$. $x_2$ takes values $\pm2$: variance $8/4=2$. $\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(8,2)$ and PC1 is the $x_1$ axis.
Change the unit of feature 2 so every value triples: $\pm2$ becomes $\pm6$. The variance grows $3\times3=9$ times, from 2 to 18.
Now $x_2$ has the larger variance, so PC1 flips to the $x_2$ axis. The ratio is $18/26=0.692$. Same students, different PC1.
Standardise instead: divide each feature by its standard deviation. Both variances become 1 and the cloud turns round.
Now $\Sigma=I$. The two PCs tie and each explains $0.5$, whatever the original units were.

scenes.title: Two points can only spread along one line

steps.caption: Two points $P=(1,2,3)$ and $Q=(3,0,5)$ in three features. Their mean is $\big(\tfrac{1+3}{2},\tfrac{2+0}{2},\tfrac{3+5}{2}\big)=(2,1,4)$.
Centre: $P-\text{mean}=(-1,1,-1)$ and $Q-\text{mean}=(1,-1,1)$.
The two centred rows add to the zero vector, so row 2 is minus row 1. Only one row is independent: rank 1.
$\Sigma=X^\top X/(n-1)$ with $n-1=1$. Every entry is $+2$ or $-2$, and every row is a copy of the first, up to sign.
The trace is $2+2+2=6$. Rank 1 means only one eigenvalue can be non-zero, so the eigenvalues are $6,\,0,\,0$.
PC1 points along the line through P and Q, direction $(-1,1,-1)/\sqrt3$. That line holds all the spread there is.
